Overview: finding nonprofit mergers in IRS 990 data

Source: vignettes/npmerger.Rmd
npmerger.Rmd

Nonprofit mergers are rare, hard to see, and easy to confuse with other ways an organization winds down. npmerger builds research datasets of mergers from IRS Form 990 e-file data:

  1. It finds candidate transactions in Schedule N.
  2. It decides which of them are mergers rather than closures or asset sales.
  3. It assembles the tables needed to study what happens to the organizations involved.

Data comes from the NCCS e-file release through panel990, and fiscal-health metrics come from fiscal.

Status. The full pipeline works, from Schedule N through the analysis tables. The classifier has not yet been validated against hand-labeled cases. See the roadmap.

What counts as a merger

Following the Wilder Research study of Minnesota mergers, a merger is the integration of two or more organizations into one legal entity, in which at least one organization ceases to exist and its programs, assets, or staff move to the successor. In 990 data that means three things have to be visible:

  • The donor closes. It files Schedule N Part I (liquidation, termination, or dissolution). Its final return usually shows assets near zero.
  • Its assets go to a nonprofit successor. One nonprofit recipient receives most of the transferred value. Assets that are scattered across many charities, or go to individuals or businesses, look like a closure.
  • People go with them. Officers, directors, or key employees join the successor.

The recipient keeps operating in almost every case, so that condition adds little information. Leadership continuity and the concentration of transferred assets are what separate a merger from a closure.

Where the evidence comes from

Schedule N. Part I lists each asset distributed by an organization that dissolved: a description, the date, fair market value (FMV), and the recipient’s name, EIN, address, and IRC section. Part II lists the same for an organization that disposed of more than 25% of its net assets and kept operating. Lines 2a–2c ask whether any officer, director, trustee, or key employee became a director, employee, or owner of the successor.

Part VII. Those Schedule N boxes are under-reported. npmerger also matches the people listed on the donor’s Part VII (years t-1 and t) against the recipient’s Part VII (years t and t+1). In 2019–21 data, 87–100% of donor–recipient pairs that checked a box shared at least one person, against 9% for closures. About 40% of asset transfers with no box checked shared people too. Leadership continuity counts when either source shows it.

Schedule N’s own text. When the asset descriptions or Part III explanation say the transfer is part of a merger or consolidation (sn_merger_pattern()), that counts as merger evidence on its own. In hand validation every terminated filing with one successor and such text read as a merger.

Corroborating disclosures. A dissolution to one nonprofit successor with no leadership evidence is promoted to a merger when at least two of these agree:

  • merger language in the donor’s Schedule O narrative;
  • merger language in the recipient’s Schedule O narrative;
  • a significant change to the recipient’s governing documents (Part VI line 4) in the merger year or the year after.

Affiliation is recorded separately from the label. It covers Schedule R links, 509(a)(3) supporting organizations, group exemptions, and chapters. About a third of two-party mergers and two-thirds of multi-party mergers happen inside one family of organizations, and many analyses will want to separate them from arm’s-length mergers.

Transaction types 

library(npmerger)
transaction_types()
#> [1] "merger2"           "mergerN"           "consolidation"    
#> [4] "asset_transfer"    "closure"           "asset_disposition"
#> [7] "reorganization"    "other"
Label Meaning
merger2 Dissolved; one dominant nonprofit successor; leadership continuity or corroboration
mergerN The same, where the successor absorbs two or more dissolving organizations
consolidation A mergerN into a newly formed entity
asset_transfer Dissolved; one dominant nonprofit successor; no continuity evidence
closure Dissolved; assets dispersed, or not going to a nonprofit
asset_disposition Part II only: more than 25% of net assets transferred, organization continues
reorganization Assets transferred to the filer’s own EIN

A first pass over 2019–21 filings (14,399 Schedule N returns) gave these shares. This was before corroboration was applied, and it used Schedule N flags or Part VII overlap as the leadership evidence:

Label Filings Share
closure 5,784 40%
asset_disposition 3,250 23%
asset_transfer 2,632 18%
merger2 2,306 16%
mergerN 427 3%

The pipeline

build_merger_data() runs everything and returns every table:

md <- build_merger_data(2019:2021, path = "PANEL990")

Each stage is also a separate function, so you can stop at any point, inspect the result, or substitute your own step:

sn  <- get_schedule_n(2019:2021)   # Schedule N tables, via panel990
tx  <- sn_transactions(sn)         # one row per asset line, Parts I and II
tx  <- recover_recipient_ein(tx, get_name_index(2018:2022))  # fill missing EINs
fl  <- sn_filings(sn, tx)          # one row per Schedule N filing
ev  <- get_evidence_tables(fl)     # 990 tables for the donors and recipients
fe  <- merger_features(fl, ev)     # add the evidence to each filing
lab <- classify_transactions(fe)   # labels plus the evidence behind them
sched_n_table(lab)                 # YEAR, OBJECTID, EIN2, TYPE, evidence

get_schedule_n() downloads about 1 MB per tax year. get_evidence_tables() is much heavier on its first run: Schedule O is about 150 MB per year and Part VII about 100 MB. Both cache what they download, and the evidence step then reads only the rows for the organizations involved.

merger_features() adds one group of columns per kind of evidence:

Function Adds Source
leader_overlap() LEADER_P7, N_SHARED_P7 Part VII names, donor t-1..t vs recipient t..t+1
add_donor_counts() N_DONORS Other dissolving donors with the same dominant successor, t±1
add_filing_history() FINAL_RETURN, DONOR_FILES_LATER, R_FORMED, R_NEW 990 header
add_corroboration() SO_MERGER_TEXT_DONOR, SO_MERGER_TEXT_RECIP, GOV_DOC_CHANGE_RECIP Schedule O, Part VI line 4
add_affiliation() AFF_SCHED_R, AFF_SUPPORT_ORG, AFF_GROUP, AFFILIATED Schedule R Part II, Schedule A, group exemption number
add_mission_similarity() MISSION_SIM Part III mission statements

Cleaning

Schedule N is messy, and the low-level helpers handle the recurring problems. Checkboxes come in several encodings:

sn_flag(c("1", "true", "X", "0", "false", NA))
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE    NA

Recipient EINs arrive in many formats, including placeholders:

clean_ein(c("01-0215911", "10215911", "000000000", "EIN-01-0215911"))
#> [1] "010215911" "010215911" NA          "010215911"
as_ein2("010215911")
#> [1] "EIN-01-0215911"

The recipient’s IRC section is free text, with dozens of spellings of 501(c)(3) alone:

parse_irc_section(c("501(c)(3)", "501 C 3", "501(c)(6)", "LLC",
                    "Individual", "City of Portland", NA))
#> [1] "501c3"        "501c3"        "other_exempt" "business"     "individual"  
#> [6] "government"   "unknown"

sn_filings() also deals with Schedule N’s header and asset tables not lining up. Some filings have only one or the other, so the filing list is built from both.

Classifying

classify_transactions() takes a filing-level table and adds a label, plus the evidence used to reach it. Here is a small made-up example with one filing of each kind:

filings <- data.frame(
  case          = c("sale", "dispersed", "flags", "part7", "corroborated", "no evidence"),
  EIN2          = paste0("EIN-01-000000", 1:6),
  HAS_P1        = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE),
  HAS_P2        = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  LEADER_SN     = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  LEADER_P7     = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
  N_NP_RECIP    = c(0L, 6L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L),
  TOP_SHARE     = c(NA, 0.2, 1, 1, 1, 1),
  TOP_RECIP_EIN = c(NA, "020000002", "020000002", "020000002", "020000002", "020000002"),
  SO_MERGER_TEXT_DONOR = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE),
  GOV_DOC_CHANGE_RECIP = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

out <- classify_transactions(filings)
out[, c("case", "LEADER", "N_CORROBORATE", "BASIS", "TYPE")]
#>            case LEADER N_CORROBORATE        BASIS              TYPE
#>          <char> <lgcl>         <int>       <char>            <char>
#> 1:         sale  FALSE             0         <NA> asset_disposition
#> 2:    dispersed  FALSE             0         <NA>           closure
#> 3:        flags   TRUE             0       leader           merger2
#> 4:        part7   TRUE             0       leader           merger2
#> 5: corroborated  FALSE             2 corroborated           merger2
#> 6:  no evidence  FALSE             0         <NA>    asset_transfer

The rules are arguments, so you can run strict and broad definitions side by side. For example, the strict definition counts only the Schedule N boxes and turns off promotion:

strict <- classify_transactions(filings, merger_rules(leader = "sn", promote = FALSE))
data.frame(case = filings$case, default = out$TYPE, strict = strict$TYPE)
#>           case           default            strict
#> 1         sale asset_disposition asset_disposition
#> 2    dispersed           closure           closure
#> 3        flags           merger2           merger2
#> 4        part7           merger2    asset_transfer
#> 5 corroborated           merger2    asset_transfer
#> 6  no evidence    asset_transfer    asset_transfer

merger_rules() also sets these thresholds and switches:

  • the minimum share of transferred value going to the dominant recipient (min_top_share, default 0.75);
  • whether a Part-II-only filing with the final-return box counts as a termination (final_as_termination, default TRUE);
  • how many dissolving donors make a merger multi-party (min_donors_n);
  • how recently a recipient must have been formed to count as a new entity (new_entity_years).

Merger identifiers

Every donor–recipient pair gets an ID of the form YEAR-FROMEIN-TOEIN, where the year is the donor’s Schedule N tax year. A group ID ties together all the donors that fold into one recipient:

merger_id(2020, "01-0215911", "010431680")
#> [1] "2020-010215911-010431680"
merger_group_id(2020, "010431680")
#> [1] "2020-010431680"

Output tables

The package ships a small extract of real 2021 filings, so the whole pipeline can run offline. Here it is run without the fiscal ratios, to keep this page quick:

ex <- npmerger_example()
md <- build_merger_data(sn = ex$sn, evidence = ex$evidence, core = ex$core,
                        names = ex$names, bmf_data = ex$bmf,
                        ratios = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
md
#> <merger_data>

#>   closure                  6

Merger cases

md$cases has one row per donor–recipient pair.

  • MERGER_YEAR is time 0 for the donor.
  • RECIP_MERGER_YEAR is time 0 for the recipient: the recipient’s tax year that contains the asset distribution date. It can differ from the donor’s year when the two keep different fiscal years.
  • MERGER_GROUP_ID and N_GROUP tie together the donors that fold into the same successor.
md$cases[, c("MERGER_ID", "MERGER_GROUP_ID", "TYPE", "MERGER_YEAR", "RECIP_MERGER_YEAR", "N_GROUP", "FMV_TO_RECIP")]
#>                    MERGER_ID MERGER_GROUP_ID          TYPE MERGER_YEAR

Value transferred

md$transfers breaks the reported fair market value down by asset class (asset_class()).

  • FMV_ASSETS excludes liabilities the recipient assumed.
  • COVERAGE compares the transfer to the donor’s beginning-of-year assets. Values far above 1 are flagged in FLAG_OUTLIER.
head(md$transfers[, c("MERGER_ID", "FMV_TOTAL", "FMV_ASSETS", "FMV_CASH", "FMV_REAL_ESTATE", "COVERAGE", "FLAG_OUTLIER")])
#>                   MERGER_ID FMV_TOTAL FMV_ASSETS FMV_CASH FMV_REAL_ESTATE
#>                      <char>     <num>      <num>    <num>           <num>

Donor and recipient attributes

md$donors and md$recipients share the merger ID and one layout:

  • SN_YEAR and REF_YEAR (time 0 on that organization’s calendar);
  • name and address;
  • formation and ruling years, and age;
  • NTEE code;
  • revenue, expenses, and assets for the five years up to REF_YEAR.
d <- md$donors
d[1:3, c("MERGER_ID", "NAME", "STATE", "AGE", "NTEE", "REVENUE_TM4", "REVENUE_TM2", "REVENUE_T0", "ASSETS_T0")]
#> Key: <MERGER_ID>
#>                   MERGER_ID                                     NAME  STATE
#>                      <char>                                   <char> <char>
#> 1: 2021-042305850-041695745  GLOUCESTER FIRE DEPARTMENT CREDIT UNION     MA
#> 2: 2021-132890752-861250084       COUNCIL FOR ADULT AND EXPERIENTIAL     IN

Part VII panel

md$part7 lists everyone on either organization’s Part VII from t-2 to t+2. IN_BOTH marks people who appear on both:

p <- md$part7
p[IN_BOTH == TRUE][1:6, c("MERGER_ID", "ROLE", "TIME_FROM_MERGER", "PERSON_NAME", "TITLE", "COMP_ORG")]
#>                   MERGER_ID   ROLE TIME_FROM_MERGER       PERSON_NAME     TITLE

Fiscal panel

md$fiscal stacks the donor’s years up to the merger and the recipient’s years before and after it, with harmonized 990 and 990-EZ measures. Overhead, executive compensation, employees, and debt detail come from the full Form 990 only.

f <- md$fiscal
f[ROLE == "recipient"][1:6, c("MERGER_ID", "TIME_FROM_MERGER", "REVENUE", "EXPENSES", "ASSETS", "STAFF_EXP", "OVERHEAD_RATIO")]
#>                   MERGER_ID TIME_FROM_MERGER   REVENUE EXPENSES     ASSETS
#>                      <char>            <int>     <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1: 2021-042305850-041695745               -5  64430195 56107971 1633755224
#> 2: 2021-042305850-041695745               -4  71469349 56395350 1682401982
#> 3: 2021-042305850-041695745               -3  79251770 64685998 1877534257
#> 4: 2021-042305850-041695745               -2  89211246 75756292 2092358761
#> 5: 2021-042305850-041695745               -1 101297996 85388608 2385374276
#> 6: 2021-042305850-041695745                0  92937477 78093785 2510941078
#>    STAFF_EXP OVERHEAD_RATIO
#>        <num>          <num>
#> 1:  22270552             NA
#> 2:  22688647             NA
#> 3:  25816134             NA
#> 4:  27518061             NA
#> 5:  33406510             NA
#> 6:  32885525             NA

With ratios = TRUE (the default), the panel also gets the ratios from fiscal::compute_all_panel(). Two choices matter when you study change over time:

  • A fixed calibration. The ratios’ winsorized and percentile variants are recomputed within each year. For an index that is comparable across years, fit fiscal::fiscal_health_fit() once on a reference sample and pass it (and fiscal::fiscal_weights()) as fit and weights.
  • Backward-looking smoothing. smooth = "trailing" averages each organization’s current and two previous years (smooth_trailing()). It never uses future years, so pre-merger values are not contaminated by post-merger ones. Use it for matching and baselines, and raw values for event-time outcomes.
